title: CPSC 541 - Chapter 3: Good Practices for Requirements Engineering

questions.question: Requirements development consists of which four major activities?
options: Project planning, writing the code, executing system tests, and deploying the finished product
Architectural design, implementing features, performing maintenance, and releasing the product
Elicitation, analysis, specification, and validation of the project's software requirements
Data modeling, programming the solution, testing the builds, and delivering user training
Budgeting the work, scheduling tasks, coding the system, and verifying the completed build
Eliciting stakeholder needs, designing the architecture, programming, and performing maintenance
questions.explanation: Chapter 3 expands on the four requirements development activities: elicitation, analysis, specification, and validation.

reference.book: Chapter 3 — A requirements development process framework
reference.excerpt: Requirements development involves elicitation, analysis, specification, and validation. These activities are interwoven, incremental, and iterative rather than a one-pass sequence.

questions.question: The four requirements development activities should always be completed in a strict sequence, with one phase completely finished before the next begins.
questions.explanation: The process should be iterative, incremental, and interleaved rather than strictly sequential.

reference.book: Chapter 3 — A requirements development process framework
reference.excerpt: Do not expect to perform elicitation, analysis, specification, and validation in a simple linear, one-pass sequence. In practice these activities are interwoven, incremental, and iterative.

questions.question: Which description best matches an iterative requirements process?
options: Requirements are written in a single pass and are never revisited after they have been recorded
Only the validation activity may be repeated; elicitation and analysis remain permanently frozen
Requirements work is postponed until implementation is finished and the product can be inspected
Teams repeatedly revisit and refine earlier requirements work as new information is discovered
Each requirements activity is performed by a completely separate team that never shares results
Requirements development activities cannot overlap and must finish before construction begins
questions.explanation: The slides show requirements work cycling back to clarify, rewrite, correct, and re-evaluate earlier information.

reference.book: Chapter 3 — A requirements development process framework
reference.excerpt: You might analyze something, realize information is missing, go back to elicitation, rewrite the specification, and validate again. Progressive refinement of detail continues throughout requirements development.

questions.question: What is one purpose of defining the requirements development process before beginning elicitation?
options: To choose the programming language and framework the developers will use for construction
To eliminate customer involvement so analysts can specify the product without interruptions
To write all acceptance test cases immediately, before any stakeholder needs have been identified
To determine the final system architecture before user classes or business goals are identified
To define the steps and activities the team will use to develop the project's requirements
To guarantee that approved requirements will never change once the process has been documented
questions.explanation: A good practice is to define the requirements development process, including its steps and activities.

reference.excerpt: Define the requirements development process so the team knows the steps and activities it will use before it begins discovering what people actually need.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a vision and scope document?
options: To describe how source code will be organized into modules, packages, and code repositories
To define the product's objectives, set the project boundaries, and keep the work focused
To list every future test case that testers will eventually execute against the finished system
To specify database indexes and physical storage details that belong in later design documents
To record only user-interface colors and branding choices rather than objectives and boundaries
To document the implementation language and coding standards the development team must follow
questions.explanation: The vision and scope document defines objectives, sets project boundaries, and helps keep the project focused.

reference.excerpt: The vision and scope document contains the product's business requirements. The vision gives stakeholders a common understanding of the outcome, and the scope defines what is in and what is out.

questions.question: Which factors can help distinguish different user classes? Select all that apply.
options: The roles that different groups of people perform when they interact with the product
The goals that different groups of people are trying to accomplish with the intended product
The features that different groups of people actually use when they work with the product
The frequency with which different groups of people use the product during their work
The knowledge and skill levels that different groups of people bring to using the product
The location and attitude of different groups of people who will use or depend on the product
questions.explanation: The slides list all of these as useful characteristics for identifying different user classes.

reference.excerpt: User groups might differ in frequency of use, features used, privilege levels, or experience. Describe aspects of their job tasks, attitudes, location, or personal characteristics that might influence product design.

questions.question: Why is identifying user classes important during elicitation?
options: Every user always wants exactly the same capabilities, so identifying classes adds little value
Identifying user classes determines which programming language the project team is required to use
Different user groups may use the system differently and therefore have different requirements
Identifying user classes replaces the need to analyze, specify, or validate the gathered requirements
Identifying user classes eliminates the need for customer representatives or product champions
Identifying user classes prevents requirements from changing after the first elicitation sessions
questions.explanation: Different user classes can have different roles, goals, skills, and usage patterns, so their requirements may differ.

reference.excerpt: To avoid overlooking the needs of any user community, identify the various groups of users for your product. Different classes can have different roles, goals, skills, and usage patterns.

questions.question: What is a product champion?
options: The developer who writes the most code and therefore decides which user needs will be implemented
A project manager whose only responsibility is to control the budget and the delivery schedule
A customer who uses the system once during a demo and then has no further project involvement
A representative of a user class who speaks for that group and may make decisions on its behalf
A tester who is solely responsible for writing and executing every acceptance test for the product
A person who must personally approve every software change regardless of its requirements impact
questions.explanation: Product champions represent user classes, speak for them, and generally make a long-term commitment to the project.

reference.excerpt: Identify an individual who can accurately serve as the voice of the customer for each user class. The product champion presents the needs of that class and makes decisions on its behalf.

questions.question: A product champion is usually expected to have a long-term commitment to the project.
questions.explanation: The slides distinguish product champions by their ongoing representation and long-term project involvement.

reference.excerpt: A product champion represents a user class over a longer period and generally makes a long-term commitment to the project, unlike a short-term focus group.

questions.question: How does a focus group differ from a product champion?
options: Focus groups write the implementation code rather than describing needed functionality and quality
Focus groups are typically short-term participants who describe functionality and quality needs
Focus groups have lasting decision-making authority over the project, unlike product champions
Focus groups permanently replace user classes and product champions for the rest of the project
Focus groups are convened only after deployment, when the product is already in production use
Focus groups exist to manage version control of requirements rather than to describe user needs
questions.explanation: Focus groups provide input about functionality and quality needs but usually have a shorter-term commitment than product champions.

reference.excerpt: Focus groups collect input on functionality and quality characteristics. Unlike product champions, focus groups generally do not have decision-making authority and usually have a shorter-term commitment.

questions.question: Use cases primarily help identify:
options: The internal class hierarchy and package structure that developers should use when writing code
The programming-language syntax and coding conventions the implementation team must follow
The detailed database schema that implementers should create instead of exploring user goals
The hardware capacity plan for production servers rather than user-system interaction sequences
Tasks users need to accomplish, their goals, and the interactions between users and the system
The project budget allocations for staff rather than the tasks users need the system to support
questions.explanation: Use cases describe tasks, goals, purposes, and interactions between users and the system.

reference.excerpt: Explore with user representatives the tasks they need to accomplish and the value they are trying to achieve. User requirements can be expressed as use cases, user stories, or scenarios that describe user-system interactions.

questions.question: Which of the following can be considered system events? Select all that apply.
options: External signals received from hardware devices or other systems outside the product boundary
Incoming data arriving from external sources that the system must accept and then process
Temporal events that occur because a scheduled time is reached rather than because of new input
Business events such as customer calls that trigger a required response from the application
Business events such as inventory changes that require the system to update stored data or react
Internal team activities such as status meetings, which are not stimuli the system itself handles
questions.explanation: The slides identify external signals and data, temporal events, and business events such as customer calls or inventory changes.

reference.excerpt: List the external events the system can experience and its expected response to each event. Event classes include signal events, temporal events, and business events such as customer calls or inventory changes.

questions.question: Why identify system events and responses during elicitation?
options: To select coding standards for the implementation rather than to reveal required system behavior
To finalize the database schema and storage design instead of discovering event-driven behavior
To understand how the system should behave when particular stimuli or external events occur
To replace user requirements with a purely technical event list that ignores stakeholder goals
To estimate only the project budget rather than to understand how the system should respond
To lock the architecture in place before any external events or expected responses are identified
questions.explanation: System events and responses help reveal required system behavior.

reference.excerpt: Identifying system events and responses shows how the product should behave based on the stimuli exercised on it. That expected reaction is the required behavior of the product.

questions.question: What is a requirements workshop?
options: A coding session in which developers implement features without discussing them with users
A closeout meeting held after deployment to review the finished product rather than draft needs
A developers-only design meeting that excludes customers and other user-class representatives
A technical performance-benchmarking session used to size servers rather than to draft needs
A budgeting workshop used to allocate funds rather than to explore and draft stakeholder needs
A collaborative session where analysts and users discuss requirements and develop draft material
questions.explanation: Workshops promote collaboration between analysts and users through discussion and draft requirements work.

reference.excerpt: Facilitated requirements-elicitation workshops that permit collaboration between analysts and customers are a powerful way to explore user needs and to draft requirements documents.

questions.question: Observing users performing their current work can help analysts understand the context for a new system.
questions.explanation: Observation can reveal current tasks, workflows, and data flows that may not be fully captured through interviews alone.

reference.excerpt: Watching users perform their business tasks establishes a context for their potential use of a new application and can reveal current tasks, workflows, and data flows.

questions.question: What useful information can be captured by observing users?
options: Only the programming languages users prefer, which watching current work is not meant to reveal
Current tasks, workflows, and data flows that show how people actually perform their work
Only future project milestone dates, which watching today's work cannot establish by itself
Implementation defects in existing code, which are found by testing rather than by job observation
Production server configuration details, which observing users perform their jobs does not reveal
Only compensation and staffing details, which do not describe current tasks or data movement
questions.explanation: Observation helps establish context and can reveal actual data flow and work practices.

reference.excerpt: Observing users performing their jobs helps analysts understand the context for a new system. Simple process-flow descriptions can depict the steps, decisions, and data movement in the current work.

questions.question: Why should analysts examine problem reports from an existing system?
options: Problem reports are useful only to testers and should be ignored during requirements elicitation
Examining problem reports prevents reuse of requirements and therefore should be avoided
Problem reports determine which programming language the team must use for the new system
Problems and requested enhancements can reveal requirements that belong in the new system
Problem reports eliminate the need to talk with users because all needs are already documented
Problem reports guarantee that the new system will contain no defects once it is released
questions.explanation: Problems with the old system and previously requested enhancements can provide valuable requirements information.

reference.excerpt: Problem reports and enhancement requests from users provide a rich source of ideas for capabilities to include in a later release or in a new product.

questions.question: What does requirements reuse mean in Chapter 3?
options: Copying all requirements from any old project without reviewing whether they still apply
Reusing only source-code modules and never considering previously written requirements text
Looking for relevant requirements from previous projects or products that may apply again
Assigning the same project manager to every effort rather than reusing applicable requirements
Avoiding all new requirements so that only reused statements are ever recorded for the product
Keeping every reused requirement unchanged forever, even when the new context is different
questions.explanation: Reuse means identifying applicable similarities with previous projects or products rather than starting from nothing.

reference.excerpt: If customers request functionality similar to that already present in an existing product, see whether the requirements are flexible enough to permit reusing or adapting applicable requirements from previous projects or products.

questions.question: What is a context diagram used for during requirements analysis?
options: To show detailed source-code structure rather than the system's place in its environment
To create acceptance test cases instead of depicting boundaries and external interfaces
To determine project staffing costs rather than to clarify the system's environmental context
To document only user stories and never the system's boundaries or external connections
To show the system's environment, its boundaries, and its interfaces to external entities
To replace the software requirements specification with a single high-level context drawing
questions.explanation: A context diagram provides a high-level view of the system, its environment, boundaries, and external interfaces.

reference.excerpt: The context diagram is a simple analysis model that shows how the new system fits into its environment. It defines the boundaries and interfaces between the system and external entities such as users, devices, and other systems.

questions.question: A prototype of a user interface can be useful because it gives users something tangible to react to and provide feedback on.
questions.explanation: The slides specifically describe UI prototypes as a way to obtain feedback on a tangible representation.

reference.excerpt: Construct a prototype to make concepts and possibilities more tangible. Prototypes let users react to something they can see and help developers and users reach a mutual understanding of the problem.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a technical prototype?
options: To create the final production product immediately instead of investigating technical risks
To explore whether uncertain or difficult technical areas of the proposed solution are feasible
To replace all requirements documentation with an informal prototype that is never written down
To decide staffing costs rather than to test whether a risky technical approach can actually work
To skip validation by treating an early technical experiment as if it were the finished design
To prevent later change requests by freezing the architecture after the first technical experiment
questions.explanation: Technical prototypes help determine whether difficult or uncertain aspects of a proposed solution are feasible.

reference.excerpt: Technical prototypes explore the feasibility of potential technical problem areas. They help determine whether difficult or uncertain aspects of a proposed solution can be implemented at acceptable cost and performance.

questions.question: Why are requirements prioritized during analysis?
options: To treat every requirement as equally important so that no item can be deferred to a later release
To eliminate customer input on value so that the team alone decides what will be built first
To select programming languages and frameworks rather than to decide what should be built first
To allocate requirements to releases and adjust when resources, needs, goals, or markets change
To prevent any future changes by freezing priorities after the first analysis workshop is finished
To avoid requirements management by assuming that priority decisions never need to be revisited
questions.explanation: Prioritization helps decide what should be implemented first and supports adjustments when circumstances change.

reference.excerpt: Prioritize requirements so the team implements the highest-value or most timely functionality first. Adjust priorities as new requirements are proposed and as customer needs, market conditions, and business goals evolve.

questions.question: Requirements modeling can help reveal which types of problems? Select all that apply.
options: Incomplete requirements that omit needed information about the intended product behavior
Inconsistent requirements that contradict one another across different statements or models
Conflicting requirements that cannot all be satisfied together in the same delivered product
Source-code naming inconsistencies, which are implementation issues rather than model defects
Unclear relationships among requirements that textual descriptions alone may leave hidden
Problems that remain hidden in natural-language descriptions until a more rigorous model is built
questions.explanation: Abstract and rigorous models can expose incompleteness, inconsistency, conflicts, and unclear relationships.

reference.excerpt: An analysis model depicts requirements visually. Models can reveal incorrect, inconsistent, missing, and conflicting requirements, as well as problems that stay hidden in natural-language descriptions.

questions.question: During analysis, teams should identify interfaces with other systems and requirements that affect other subsystems.
questions.explanation: The slides include identification of external interfaces and requirements allocated to other subsystems as analysis activities.

reference.excerpt: All software systems have connections to other parts of the world through external interfaces. Analysis includes identifying those interfaces and allocating requirements that affect other subsystems.

questions.question: What is one major goal of requirements specification?
options: To replace ongoing customer communication with a written document that is never discussed again
To create the final source code directly from notes instead of recording reviewable requirements
To create requirements documentation that is consistent, accessible, and reviewable by stakeholders
To eliminate change management by assuming that a written specification will never be updated
To perform product deployment activities rather than to document analyzed requirements clearly
To reduce the number of stakeholders who may review or comment on the written requirements
questions.explanation: Specification should produce requirements documentation that can be consistently understood, accessed, and reviewed.

reference.excerpt: The essence of requirements specification is to document requirements of different types in a consistent, accessible, and reviewable way that the intended audiences can readily understand.

questions.question: What kind of document template is suggested in the slides for software requirements specifications?
options: A detailed design-document template that records class diagrams instead of software requirements
A project-charter template that records only schedule and budget rather than specified requirements
A test-plan template that organizes test cases instead of structuring the software requirements
A coding-standards template that lists programming conventions rather than requirement sections
A deployment-runbook template that describes release steps instead of specifying product requirements
An IEEE 830-style software requirements specification template used for consistent documentation
questions.explanation: The slides explicitly mention adopting an SRS template such as IEEE 830.

reference.excerpt: Adopt standard templates for documenting requirements, including an SRS template. The course materials specifically mention an IEEE 830-style software requirements specification template.

questions.question: Why should the source or origin of a requirement be recorded?
options: To determine which programmer must write the code rather than why the requirement is needed
To eliminate requirements validation because a recorded source is treated as automatically correct
To prevent future discussion of the requirement once its origin has been written down once
To calculate required server capacity rather than to explain why the requirement is present
To justify why the requirement exists and to support later clarification with the originator
To determine the programming language rather than to enable later contact with the originator
questions.explanation: Recording sources helps explain the requirement's presence and allows analysts to return to the originator when clarification is needed.

reference.excerpt: To ensure that stakeholders know why every requirement is needed, trace each one back to its origin. Recording the source lets analysts return to the originator when clarification is needed.

questions.question: Why should individual requirements have unique identifiers?
options: To make requirements harder to read by adding identifiers that provide no management value
To support traceability, referencing, and management of individual requirements over time
To identify the programmer who wrote each requirement rather than to enable later tracing
To eliminate change requests by treating a labeled requirement as permanently unchangeable
To replace the software requirements specification with a list of identifiers and nothing else
To improve runtime system performance, which unique requirement labels cannot actually do
questions.explanation: Unique IDs help trace, manage, reference, and track individual requirements.

reference.excerpt: Give each requirement a unique identifying label. Labeling permits requirements traceability, referencing, and the recording of changes made to individual requirements.

questions.question: According to the slides, business rules should generally be kept separate from the SRS because:
options: They are unimportant to software projects and therefore do not need to be recorded anywhere at all
They apply only to programmers and have no implications for functional requirements or policies
They are always temporary project notes and never outlive the software effort that first recorded them
They can exist beyond the scope of a single software project and should be treated as enterprise assets
They are only test cases and should be stored with the test suite rather than as business rules
They cannot influence software requirements and therefore need no traceability links to the SRS
questions.explanation: Business rules often exist independently of a particular software application or project.

reference.excerpt: Document business rules separately from a project's requirements because they typically have an existence beyond the scope of a specific project. Treat them as an enterprise-level asset, not only a project-level asset.

questions.question: Which of the following are quality attributes emphasized in the specification section? Select all that apply.
options: Performance characteristics that describe how timely or responsive the product must be in use
Efficiency characteristics that describe how economically the product uses computing resources
Reliability characteristics that describe how dependably the finished product continues to operate
Robustness characteristics that describe how well the product handles unexpected conditions
Usability characteristics that describe how readily intended users can learn and operate the product
Project staffing levels, which are resource concerns rather than specified product quality attributes
questions.explanation: The slides list performance, efficiency, reliability, robustness, and usability as important quality attributes.

reference.excerpt: Go beyond functionality to specify quality characteristics that matter for success, including performance, efficiency, reliability, robustness, and usability.

questions.question: What is one validation practice described in Chapter 3?
options: Rewrite the source code of the product instead of examining the written requirements for defects
Remove customer involvement from the reviews so that only developers inspect the requirements
Inspect requirements documents through formal or informal reviews to find defects, omissions, and gaps
Freeze all requirements permanently so that validation never has to be repeated after the first pass
Choose the final database product instead of checking whether the documented requirements are right
Deploy the finished system to production instead of validating the requirements before construction
questions.explanation: Validation includes formal and informal inspection of requirements documents.

reference.excerpt: Validation asks whether the right requirements were documented. Practices include formal inspections, informal reviews, and other examinations of the requirements documents.

questions.question: What distinguishes a formal requirements inspection?
options: It is performed by only one developer working alone without other stakeholder perspectives
It occurs only after the product has already been deployed and users have begun to report defects
It replaces customer review entirely so that users never examine the written requirements themselves
It requires no written documentation and can be completed from memory of earlier conversations
It is a rigorous examination that involves people with different perspectives and areas of expertise
It focuses only on programming style rather than on whether the documented requirements are correct
questions.explanation: Formal inspection is a structured review involving multiple perspectives and areas of expertise.

reference.excerpt: Peer review of requirements, particularly the rigorous review called inspection, assembles reviewers who represent different perspectives and carefully examine the written requirements for defects.

questions.question: Which activities are associated with defining test cases during validation? Select all that apply.
options: Describe the expected behavior of the product under specified conditions using derived test cases
Review the derived test cases with customers or users to confirm that they reflect true expectations
Trace each test case back to the specification to confirm coverage and to find overlooked requirements
Define acceptance criteria that describe how users will decide whether the solution is fit for use
Select the implementation language, which is a design decision rather than a requirements validation activity
Delete the requirements baseline so that test cases can replace the written specification entirely
questions.explanation: The slides connect test cases to expected behavior, customer review, traceability, and acceptance criteria.

reference.excerpt: Derive tests from the user requirements to document expected behavior, walk through those tests with customers, map tests to the specification, and define acceptance criteria for fitness for use.

questions.question: Requirements management primarily focuses on:
options: Writing the application's source code rather than controlling changes to established requirements
Controlling and tracking changes to requirements after they have been established and baselined
Designing the physical database rather than tracking changes to the agreed requirements set
Creating the user-interface layouts rather than managing change to the established requirements
Hiring additional developers rather than controlling and tracking approved requirements changes
Replacing requirements development entirely instead of managing change after requirements exist
questions.explanation: Once requirements are established, management is largely about controlling and tracking change.

reference.excerpt: Requirements management encompasses practices that help you deal with requirements after you have them in hand, including version control, baselining, change control, status tracking, and tracing requirements to other system elements.

questions.question: What are the three main steps mentioned for a change control process?
options: Coding the change, testing the build, and deploying the result without a change-control decision
Eliciting new needs, designing the architecture, and implementing code as the change-control path
Planning the schedule, budgeting the work, and hiring staff instead of proposing and resolving changes
Requesting a change, immediately coding it, and releasing it without analysis or board resolution
Drafting comments, compiling the program, and testing the build as if that were change control
Proposal of the change, analysis of its impact, and resolution of whether to accept the change
questions.explanation: The slide describes a change control process consisting of proposal, analysis, and resolution.

reference.excerpt: Establish a mechanism so requirements changes are proposed, analyzed, and resolved. Manage all proposed changes through this process rather than hoping changes will not happen.

questions.question: What is a Change Control Board (CCB)?
options: A meeting of all customers that must vote on every change before any analysis is performed
A programming team that implements every requested change without evaluating project impact
A small, competent, empowered group that decides how proposed requirements changes are handled
A testing team that decides requirements changes based only on how hard the change is to test
A hardware-selection committee that chooses servers rather than evaluating requirements changes
A documentation archive that stores old specifications but does not decide how changes are handled
questions.explanation: The CCB evaluates and makes decisions about proposed requirements changes.

reference.excerpt: Charter a small group of project stakeholders as a change control board to evaluate proposed requirements changes, decide which ones to accept, and set implementation priorities or target releases.

questions.question: What does change impact analysis evaluate? Select all that apply.
options: Other development artifacts that would have to change if the proposed requirement change is accepted
The effort required to perform the tasks needed to implement the proposed requirements change
The estimated cost of implementing the proposed change, including work on related system elements
The scope of the proposed change across requirements, design, code, tests, and other related work
Only whether the customer likes the idea, without evaluating effort, cost, scope, or related artifacts
Potential effects on related system elements that traceability links show may also need modification
questions.explanation: Impact analysis looks at the scope of the proposed change, related artifacts, effort, cost, and broader effects.

reference.excerpt: Evaluate each proposed requirement change to assess its effect on the project, including related artifacts, the effort and cost required, the scope of the change, and potential effects on related system elements.

questions.question: Why are baseline and version control important in requirements management?
options: They prevent all requirements changes rather than controlling which versions are official baselines
They replace the need for requirements traceability once a baseline identifier has been assigned
They eliminate customer communication after the first baseline is published for a given release
They help distinguish release baselines and tell previous requirement versions from current ones
They remove the need to keep a change history once version identifiers have been assigned
They determine runtime system performance, which baseline and version labels cannot affect
questions.explanation: Baseline and version control help teams know which set of requirements belongs to which release and what changed between versions.

reference.excerpt: A baseline defines an agreed-upon set of requirements, typically for a specific release. Unique version identifiers help avoid confusion between drafts and baselines and between previous and current versions.

questions.question: A requirements change history should allow the team to know which four things?
options: What changed in the requirement, when it changed, who made each change, and why the change was made
Which source module was edited, how many lines changed, which release received it, and who coded it
Which server hosted it, which database stored it, which framework ran it, and which language was used
Which stakeholder requested it, which meeting recorded it, which tool stored it, and which file held it
What tests passed afterward, who executed them, which environment was used, and which build shipped
Only the latest requirement wording, without recording the date, the author, or the reason for change
questions.explanation: The slides specifically say a change history should capture the what, when, who, and why.

reference.excerpt: Retain a history of changes made to individual requirements. Record the dates that requirements were changed, the changes that were made, who made each change, and why.

questions.question: Which sequence contains valid requirements change statuses from the slides?
options: Written, coded, deployed, and deleted, which are not the change-status values given in the chapter
Planned, designed, compiled, and shipped, which describe construction rather than change-request status
Requested, documented, ignored, and archived, which omit approval, implementation, and verification
Drafted, tested, fixed, and maintained, which are not the status sequence identified in the slides
Proposed, approved, implemented, and verified as the requirement change moves through development
Analyzed, programmed, hosted, and monitored, which describe later life-cycle work rather than change status
questions.explanation: The transcript and slides identify proposed, approved, implemented, and verified as example change states.

reference.excerpt: Track the status of each requirement, including states such as proposed, approved, implemented, or verified, so you can monitor how each change request is moving through development.

questions.question: What does requirements volatility measure?
options: The system's response time under load, which is a performance attribute rather than change rate
The rate at which requirements are changing during the project, not a measure of system speed
The defect density found in source code, which measures implementation quality rather than change rate
The number of developers assigned to the team, which does not measure how frequently needs change
The measured level of customer satisfaction, which is not the definition of requirements volatility
The volume of data stored by the product, which does not describe how frequently requirements change
questions.explanation: Volatility refers to how frequently or rapidly requirements change.

reference.excerpt: Requirements management includes measuring requirements volatility, the rate at which requirements are changing, along with the reasons those changes are occurring.

questions.question: High requirements volatility can indicate which possible problems? Select all that apply.
options: A poor understanding of the real requirements, which can cause frequent corrections and churn
An ill-defined project scope, which leaves the boundary unstable and invites constant change
Changing business conditions that force the team to revise previously agreed requirements
Organizational or political issues that drive repeated changes unrelated to genuine product need
Guaranteed project success, which high volatility does not indicate and often works against
Possible instability in the requirements process that allows uncontrolled change to continue
questions.explanation: The slides mention poor understanding, weak scope definition, business dynamics, and politics as possible causes of high volatility.

reference.excerpt: High change rates can indicate poor understanding of the requirements, an ill-defined project scope, changing business conditions, organizational or political issues, or instability in the requirements process.

questions.question: Why might a requirements management tool be useful?
options: A tool removes the need for requirements analysts because the software can elicit needs by itself
A tool prevents every future defect, which no requirements-management product can actually do
A tool makes customer involvement unnecessary because stakeholders no longer need to review needs
A tool eliminates the need to write requirements because the repository invents them automatically
A tool automatically decides which features are correct without human analysis or validation
Automation can reduce repetitive work and support tracking, versioning, and traceability tasks
questions.explanation: The slides note that tools can eliminate drudgery and help perform requirements management tasks more effectively.

reference.excerpt: Commercial requirements management tools store requirements in a database and help implement and automate tracking, versioning, change history, and traceability tasks, reducing repetitive manual work.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a requirements traceability matrix?
options: To store stakeholder contact lists rather than to link requirements to later development artifacts
To replace the source-code repository so that design and tests no longer need any other storage
To connect each requirement to the design, code, and tests that implement and verify that requirement
To calculate the project budget and staffing cost rather than to link requirements through artifacts
To document only business objectives and never their connections to design, code, or test cases
To track project budget line items, which is a cost-accounting concern rather than requirements tracing
questions.explanation: A traceability matrix links requirements through later development artifacts.

reference.excerpt: A requirements traceability matrix is a set of links that connect each functional requirement to the design and code elements that implement it and the tests that verify it.

questions.question: Which benefits can a traceability matrix provide? Select all that apply.
options: Help ensure that required functionality is not missed during design, construction, and testing
Connect each requirement to the code and tests that implement and verify that requirement
Help prevent unwanted features from appearing when they have no approved requirement source
Support tracking of requirements as they move through development and later change activity
Guarantee that the delivered product will have zero defects, which no matrix can actually ensure
Show how requirements flow through design, implementation, and test so gaps can be found
questions.explanation: Traceability helps ensure required work is implemented and prevents functionality with no requirement justification from being added.

reference.excerpt: A traceability matrix helps confirm that required functionality is implemented and verified, supports tracking through development, and helps stop developers from adding unauthorized features.

questions.question: A developer adds a feature that cannot be traced back to any approved requirement. What problem can traceability help reveal?
options: A missing project manager, which traceability of features to requirements does not reveal
A hardware manufacturing defect, which a requirements-to-code trace matrix does not detect
A user-training gap, which is not what missing requirement-to-feature traces are meant to expose
An extraneous or unauthorized feature that was added without an approved requirement source
A database-indexing problem, which is a design-performance issue rather than a tracing finding
A requirements baseline that automatically fails, which is not the problem this scenario describes
questions.explanation: Traceability can expose features that were added without an approved requirement.

reference.excerpt: Traceability keeps requirements from being forgotten and stops developers from adding unauthorized features. A feature that cannot be traced to an approved requirement is extraneous.

questions.question: Which statement best summarizes the overall Chapter 3 process?
options: Develop requirements iteratively through elicitation, analysis, specification, and validation, then manage changes in a controlled and traceable way
Write every requirement in a single linear pass, freeze that document so it cannot change, and only then allow the construction work to begin
Let customers define all technical design and architecture choices, skipping a disciplined requirements development and change-management process
Skip analysis and specification entirely and rely only on prototypes, without validating a reviewable requirements baseline for the product
Focus only on requirements management activities and skip elicitation, analysis, specification, and validation of the actual product needs
Complete all programming of the product first, and only afterward validate whether the documented requirements were actually correct ones
questions.explanation: Chapter 3 presents requirements engineering as an iterative development process followed by disciplined requirements management.

reference.book: Chapter 3 — A requirements development process framework
reference.excerpt: Requirements development is iterative through elicitation, analysis, specification, and validation. Requirements management then deals with those requirements after you have them, using change control and tracing.
